'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.

'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.

'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.

'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.

'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.

'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)-qq]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Yunomine Ōji (湯の峰王子) === {{See|Yunomine Ōji}}
== References == {{Reflist|2}}
== Related Pages == * {{ill|Kumano faith|ja|熊野信仰}} * {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} * {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.
== Access == * **Nearest Station:** {{ill|Shingū Station|ja|新宮駅}} (JR {{ill|Kisei Main Line|ja|紀勢本線}}) * Bus services from {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}} via {{ill|Ryujin Bus|ja|龍神バス}}

'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq-{{subst:MAINSPACE}}--qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)-qq]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Yunomine Ōji (湯の峰王子) === {{See|Yunomine Ōji}}
== References == {{Reflist|2}}
== Related Pages == * {{ill|Kumano faith|ja|熊野信仰}} * {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} * {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.
== Access == * **Nearest Station:** {{ill|Shingū Station|ja|新宮駅}} (JR {{ill|Kisei Main Line|ja|紀勢本線}}) * Bus services from {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}} via {{ill|Ryujin Bus|ja|龍神バス}}

'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)-qq]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.

'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)-qq]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.

'''List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市本宮町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市本宮町)-qq]] [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}} | Image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | Location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | Coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }} [[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Kujūku Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Kujūku Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama)|ja|音無川}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|ja|湯の峰温泉}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* Location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* Location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|ja|熊野本宮大社}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原}}.
* Location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* Location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}}.
