'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Hongū Town)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hongū, Wakayama|1=Q11520136|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11520136}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Ninety-Nine Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17050475}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mitsukoshi Pass|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Nakahechi Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370053}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama|ja|音無川|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otonashi River (Wakayama|1=Q11664306|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11664306}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Akagigoe|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Nakahechi Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370053}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|en|Yunomine Onsen|WD=Q11563414|lt=Yunomine Onsen|1=Yunomine Onsen}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hagi, Hongū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|en|Kishū Domain|WD=Q1069187|lt=Kishū Domain|1=Kishū Domain}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūyūki|qq=}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yorimotoki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gōdōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosshinmon Ōji|1=Hosshinmon Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3141012}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūyūki|qq=}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Engi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōji-ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en|Kumano Hongū Taisha|WD=Q705035|lt=Kumano Hongū Taisha|1=Kumano Hongū Taisha}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyunohara|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.
* location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kohechi|1=Kohechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11463835}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kuki, Hongū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|WD=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|WD=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}}.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市本宮町)]]
This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|田辺市本宮町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hongū, Wakayama|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}
==Overview== {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | Name = {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Hongū Town)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} | image = [[File:HOSSHINMON-oji.JPG|thumb|250px|right|Hossinmon Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|lt=Wakayama Prefecture|1=Wakayama Prefecture}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|45|N|135|45|30|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰|1=Kumano Faith|2=ja|3=熊野信仰|WD=Q135501741}}{{efn|The religion of [[Kumano Shrines]]|1=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Three Shrines|lt=Kumano faith|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = | location = {{ill|Tanabe|WD=Q304266|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} }}
'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Hongū Town)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hongū, Wakayama|1=Q11520136|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11520136}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Ninety-Nine Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17050475}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mitsukoshi Pass|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Nakahechi Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370053}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama|ja|音無川|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otonashi River (Wakayama|1=Q11664306|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11664306}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Akagigoe|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Nakahechi Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370053}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|en|Yunomine Onsen|WD=Q11563414|lt=Yunomine Onsen|1=Yunomine Onsen}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hagi, Hongū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|en|Kishū Domain|WD=Q1069187|lt=Kishū Domain|1=Kishū Domain}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūyūki|qq=}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yorimotoki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gōdōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosshinmon Ōji|1=Hosshinmon Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3141012}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūyūki|qq=}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Engi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōji-ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en|Kumano Hongū Taisha|WD=Q705035|lt=Kumano Hongū Taisha|1=Kumano Hongū Taisha}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyunohara|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.
* location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kohechi|1=Kohechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11463835}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kuki, Hongū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|WD=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|WD=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}}.

'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Hongū Town)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the former {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|ja|本宮町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hongū, Wakayama|1=Q11520136|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11520136}} area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|qid=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q30074932}} of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|qid=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|qid=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|qid=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Ninety-Nine Ōji of Hongū-chō, Tanabe City (田辺市本宮町の九十九王子) ==
There are six '''Ninety-Nine Ōji''' shrines within the Hongū-chō area of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|qid=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}. All of these are part of the national historic site, the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17050475}}, designated on November 2, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|ja |url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html |title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments |publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education |accessdate=2009-03-20 }}</ref>
After crossing the {{ill|Mitsukoshi Pass|ja|三越峠|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mitsukoshi Pass|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Nakahechi Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11370053}}, the pilgrimage route enters the inner Kumano area, descending along the upper reaches of the {{ill|Otonashi River (Wakayama|ja|音無川|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otonashi River (Wakayama|1=Q11664306|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11664306}}. During the early modern period, a ridge path known as the {{ill|Akagigoe|ja|赤木越|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Akagigoe|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City, Nakahechi Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11370053}}, which shortcuts between this pass and {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|en|Yunomine Onsen|qid=Q11563414|lt=Yunomine Onsen|1=Yunomine Onsen}}, came into use. However, due to landslides on the Mitsukoshi Pass side, it is no longer possible to traverse the entire route.
=== Inohana Ōji (猪鼻王子) === [[File:INOHANA-oji monument.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Inohana Ōji]]
'''Inohana Ōji''' (猪鼻王子) is located along the banks of the Otonashi River, sourced from the area around Mitsukoshi Pass. The pilgrimage route has largely disappeared due to forest road development connecting {{ill|Hagi, Hongū|ja|本宮町萩|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hagi, Hongū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to Mitsukoshi Pass. To reach the shrine site, one must descend from the forest road to the riverbank. Today, only a stone monument erected by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|en|Kishū Domain|qid=Q1069187|lt=Kishū Domain|1=Kishū Domain}} remains.
The shrine is mentioned as "Inohana" in the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and both the {{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūyūki|qq=}} and {{ill|Yorimotoki|ja|頼資卿記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yorimotoki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} note that the pilgrimage crossed the stream several times before reaching Inohana Ōji.<ref>Heibonsha [1997: 99]</ref> The shrine fell into disuse following the decline of Kumano pilgrimages. The {{ill|Gōdōki|ja|郷導記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gōdōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} also describes crossing a plank bridge over the valley stream, suggesting that the path remained unchanged for a long time. Although it is believed that pilgrims once ascended a mountain path from near Inohana Ōji toward the next shrine, {{ill|Hosshinmon Ōji|ja|発心門王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hosshinmon Ōji|1=Hosshinmon Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3141012}}, this route can no longer be traced today.
* location: 1811 Inohana, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Hosshinmon Ōji (発心門王子) === {{See|Hosshinmon Ōji}}
=== Mizunomi Ōji (水呑王子) === [[File:Monument of MIZUNOMI-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Mizunomi Ōji Monument]]
After descending from Hosshinmon Ōji along the forest road and passing through a small settlement, one arrives at Hagi in Hongū-chō. Proceeding along a local road within the settlement and ascending a forest road for just under 2 km leads to the site of '''Mizunomi Ōji''' (水呑王子), where a green schist stone monument stands.
According to the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja|和歌山県聖蹟|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wakayama Prefecture Sacred Sites|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the name "Mizunomi Ōji" derives from the {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and it remains known by this name today. However, medieval pilgrimage records ({{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūyūki|qq=}}, {{ill|Guki|ja|愚記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) explicitly refer to it as "Uchi Mizunomi Ōji," a name also found in the {{ill|Kumano Engi|ja|熊野縁起|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Engi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and the {{ill|Ōji-ki|ja|王子記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōji-ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.<ref name="Kumanoji_1973_137">Kumanonji Editorial Committee [1973: 137]</ref> This suggests it was known as "Uchi Mizunomi" until around the late 16th century.
* location: 1416-1 Ōyokote, Mitsukoshi, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Fushiogami Ōji (伏拝王子) === [[File:FUSHIOGAMI-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Fushiogami Ōji Shrine]] [[File:Izumi-Shikibu memorial monument.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Izumi Shikibu Memorial Tower]]
After passing the former site of the branch school, the pilgrimage route continues along a dirt path, emerging into the settlement of Fushiogami. At the top of the hill in the Chaya district stands '''Fushiogami Ōji''' (伏拝王子). Here, pilgrims, after their long and arduous journey, could catch their first glimpse of the sacred forest of the old site of {{ill|Kumano Hongū Taisha|en|Kumano Hongū Taisha|qid=Q705035|lt=Kumano Hongū Taisha|1=Kumano Hongū Taisha}}, known as {{ill|Ōyunohara|ja|大斎原|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyunohara|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.
* location: 157 Chayazoku, Fushiogami, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City
=== Haraido Ōji (祓戸王子) === [[File:HARAIDO-oji.JPG|thumb|right|120px|Haraido Ōji Shrine]] [[File:The grove of HARAIDO-oji.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Sacred Grove of Haraido Ōji]] [[File:Milestone Naka-no-daira.jpg|thumb|right|120px|Milestone at Sangen Chaya]]
Beyond Fushiogami Ōji, the route transitions back to a dirt path, merging with the {{ill|Kohechi|ja|小辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kohechi|1=Kohechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11463835}} at {{ill|Kuki, Hongū|ja|本宮町九鬼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kuki, Hongū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The confluence once housed a checkpoint and teahouses, now known as the site of Sangen Chaya. Continuing along the ridge path and descending the final slope through a residential area reveals a small, dome-shaped grove. Nestled within is '''Haraido Ōji''' (祓戸王子), also recorded as "Haraiden" or "Haraisho" in historical documents.
* location: 1077 Haraido, Hongū-chō, Tanabe City

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|qid=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|qid=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}}.
